title: College Career Closets: Sizing, Donations & Access Guide
summary: A practical guide for career services teams building or improving a career closet. Learn how to manage donations, plan inclusive sizing, decide what to stock, set access rules, prepare for high-demand periods, and use examples from colleges already running professional clothing programs.
body_markdown:
If you run a career closet, the hardest part is usually not collecting clothes. It is making sure students can find something appropriate, in the right size, at the moment they actually need it.


A closet can be full and still fail students if inventory is uneven, donations are outdated, access rules are too restrictive, or the most-needed sizes disappear before career fairs and interview season.


While relying only on donations can also leave career centers with too much of what students do not need and too little of what they do.


This guide explains how career centers can build or improve a career closet, including what to stock, how to source and manage donations, how to handle inclusive sizing, what access rules to set, and how to connect the program to interviews, career fairs, internships, and other high-demand moments, with examples from colleges already running these programs.


## What Should a Career Closet Operating Model Include?


A useful career closet needs seven things to work together: a clear access model, targeted inventory, size-gap tracking, strict donation rules, multiple ways to access clothing, connections to high-demand career moments, and a small set of metrics showing whether students actually found what they needed.


Here is a practical starting model.


Operating decision Strong starting point What to avoid


Student eligibility Make clothing broadly available unless funding requires need-based eligibility Requiring students to prove hardship for donated clothing


Clothing model Let students keep common basics; use borrowing, rental, or financial support for higher-cost gaps Assuming one model has to cover every student


Inventory Organize around actual career occasions and size demand Measuring success by the total number of garments


Donations Publish a current needs list and reject unusable items Accepting every professional-looking donation


Sizing Track shortages by garment type and size Saying "all sizes welcome" without measuring availability


Access Combine regular hours with appointments, drop-ins, and event pop-ups Making students wait weeks for clothing needed tomorrow


Measurement Track complete-outfit rate, unmet need, stockouts, and reason for visit Reporting only donations received or students checked in


The important shift is simple: **manage the closet around student demand rather than donated supply.**


## Why Should Career Centers Treat Professional Clothing as an Access Issue?


Career centers should treat professional clothing as an access issue because many students are already making difficult choices about basic expenses. A professional outfit can become another cost students have to absorb precisely when they are trying to[access internships](https://www.hiration.com/blog/paid-unpaid-internships-policy-guide-higher-ed/) , career fairs, interviews, and other opportunities connected to post-college employment.


According to The[Hope Center's 2023-2024 Student Basic Needs Survey](https://hope.temple.edu/research/hope-center-basic-needs-survey/2023-2024-student-basic-needs-survey-report) , **59% of 74,350 respondents across 91 institutions experienced food or housing insecurity** . The same study found 41% experienced food insecurity, 48% housing insecurity, and 14% homelessness.


Professional clothing is obviously not equivalent to food or housing. But those numbers give career centers useful context when deciding whether students can simply be expected to buy clothing for recruiting activities.


In some cases, clothing directly affects access to the event itself.


For example, the[Texas A&M Student Engineers' Council](https://careerfair.sec.tamu.edu/career-fair/students/fair-information/dress-code) requires professional attire for its in-person career fair and states that students who do not comply will not be admitted.


Texas A&M pairs the requirement with access to a Career Closet and has offered a Career Closet pop-up in the engineering complex before the fair.


That is an important operating principle.


If a career center, academic college, recruiter event, conference, or campus partner expects a particular level of dress, students should know where they can access it before the event.


## Should Students Keep, Borrow, Rent, or Receive Money for Professional Clothing?


The right model depends on what your center can reliably supply. Free-to-keep closets are simple for students but require constant replenishment. Lending stretches expensive inventory further but adds returns and cleaning. Financial assistance gives students more choice.[A hybrid model](https://www.hiration.com/blog/organizational-structure-models-career-centers-higher-ed/) lets career centers use each option where it works best.


There are already several models in use across higher education.


\`\`\` Model University example How it works Useful when


Free to keep[University of Florida](https://careerhub.ufl.edu/resources/career-closet/) Students can currently receive one full professional outfit You have recurring donations and storage capacity


Limited free items[Kansas State University](https://www.k-state.edu/careercenter/students/apply_interview/attire/) Students can typically take up to three items depending on inventory You want a simple inventory cap


Borrowing[University of Utah](https://careers.utah.edu/career-closet/) More than 920 garments are available for students to borrow You can manage returns and cleaning


Clothing scholarship[University of Georgia](https://career.uga.edu/scholarships_and_programs) Eligible students can receive $200 toward professional clothing Students need more choice in size, fit, or style


Rental/subscription[Georgetown University](https://careercenter.georgetown.edu/about-us/career-closet/) Students can access up to six items for a month through a clothing-rental model Maintaining sufficient campus inventory is difficult


Remote purchase/fulfillment[UC Clermont](https://www.ucclermont.edu/students/careers/career-closet.html) Students can receive up to $150 in clothing and can request items shipped home You serve commuters or students who cannot visit the closet


The University of Georgia's approach is particularly useful when donated inventory cannot reliably meet individual needs.


Its Dawgs Suit Up Scholarship provides $200 to students with documented financial need, and UGA says as many as 700 scholarship awards have been distributed in a year.


Awards are also timed before fall and spring career fair periods.


Georgetown solves the inventory problem differently. Its[Cawley Career Closet](https://careercenter.georgetown.edu/about-us/career-closet/) uses a rental service through which students can access **six items for one month** , with need-based funding available.


Career centers therefore do not need to force every student into the same closet model.


A useful hybrid could be:


- Free donated shirts, blouses, ties, trousers, skirts, and basic blazers
- A smaller lending inventory for suits and higher-value pieces
- A purchasing fund for sizes the closet cannot supply
- Emergency gift cards for students with an interview or start date approaching
- External rental or retail partnerships when internal inventory cannot solve the need


That gives the center more ways to solve the actual problem: **getting the student an appropriate outfit in time.**


## What Should a College Career Closet Actually Stock?


Career centers should build inventory around professional situations rather than around a generic list of "professional clothes." A career fair, interview, case competition, presentation, networking dinner, and first week at an internship can require different combinations. Stocking versatile separates usually gives students more usable combinations than concentrating heavily on matching suits.


Start with the career moments your students encounter most.


Career moment Priority inventory Easy-to-miss items


Interview Blazers, suit separates, dress shirts, blouses, trousers, skirts, dresses Belts, ties, socks, shoes, portfolios


Career fair Professional separates that can be worn for several hours Comfortable professional footwear


Networking event Business-casual separates Cardigans, chinos, simple accessories


Presentation or case competition Jackets, trousers, skirts, dresses, shirts Items that work while sitting and presenting


Conference Mix-and-match pieces for multiple days More than one shirt or top


Internship or first job Repeatable business-casual combinations Pieces that work across several outfits


Professional headshot Camera-ready tops and jackets Neutral options across multiple sizes


This is one reason a closet audit should count **complete combinations** , not only individual garments.


28 ties and 19 blazers may look like healthy inventory. But, they are not useful to a student if the closet has no trousers or shirts in that student's size.


[Kansas State](https://www.k-state.edu/careercenter/students/apply_interview/attire/) puts another useful limit on donations: clothing should generally have been **purchased within the past five years and remain current with professional fashion** .


The[University of Houston-Clear Lake](https://eportfolio.uhcl.edu/career-development/students/career-closet) takes a similar approach, requesting clothing purchased within the past five years and rejecting items that need repairs or arrive with stains, odors, missing buttons, or other problems.


Those rules matter because every poor-quality donation creates work.


Someone has to receive it, inspect it, sort it, store it, move it, and eventually dispose of or redirect it.


A smaller closet with usable inventory can be more valuable than a large closet filled with items students rarely choose.


## How Can Career Centers Make Inclusive Sizing Work in a Donation-Based Closet?


Inclusive sizing requires inventory data, not an inclusive statement on the website. Track availability by garment and size, publish major gaps when useful, allocate money specifically for recurring shortages, and give students another route when the donated inventory cannot serve them.


[Virginia Tech](https://career.vt.edu/channels/career-outfitters/) provides a useful example.


Its Career Outfitters program publicly lists sizes as **available, limited, or unavailable** rather than simply saying that it carries different sizes.


Its current inventory page, for example, lists shortages across both ends of the size range, including several XXS, XS, and XXXL categories. Virginia Tech also accepts monetary donations specifically to purchase **high-demand and out-of-stock sizes** that clothing donations fail to provide.


That is a much stronger system than counting total garments. A simple size-gap tracker can look like this:


Item Size Students requesting Available now Unable to serve Action


Blazer Example: XS 12 2 7 Priority purchase


Trousers Example: 40-42 9 1 6 Add to donor wish list


Dress shoes Example: 11 7 0 5 Purchase


Blouse Example: XL 14 9 1 Monitor


The numbers above are examples. Your own data should determine purchasing.


### Track failed searches, not only successful checkouts


The most useful number may be the student who leaves with nothing. Add one question at checkout or after a visit:


**"Were you able to find an outfit you could actually wear for the event you came in for?"**


If not, record:


- garment needed
- size needed
- type of event
- date needed
- whether an alternative solution was provided


Within a semester, the center has a purchasing list created by actual student demand.


### Expand inclusion beyond standard size ranges


UHCL specifically includes **maternity professional clothing** on its donation needs list.


The[University of Florida](https://careerhub.ufl.edu/resources/dress-for-success-guide/) states that its Career Closet includes **gender-neutral and inclusive styles** and offers individualized support based on students' clothing needs and style preferences.


The practical question is not whether the closet welcomes everyone.


It is whether a student with a particular body, style, cultural preference, or professional context can actually find something they can use.


## How Should Career Centers Manage Donations Without Turning the Closet Into Storage?


Career centers should accept donations against an inventory plan. Publish what you need now, establish minimum condition and recency standards, pause categories you already have too many of, and create a route for rejected or surplus items. The goal is not to collect the most clothing. It is to maintain useful inventory.


Virginia Tech provides one of the clearest examples of targeted donation requests.


Rather than asking broadly for professional clothing, Career Outfitters publishes urgent needs including specific garment types and size ranges. Its current list identifies needs such as suit jackets, dress pants, shirts, shoes, belts, ties, blazers, and blouses, with exact size ranges.


Career centers can copy that approach.


Instead of:


**"Donate professional attire to our Career Closet."**


Use:


**"September priority: blazers in sizes X-Y, dress pants in sizes X-Y, professional shoes, simple belts, and long-sleeve shirts."**


That gives alumni, faculty, staff, employers, and community donors a much better chance of sending something useful.


### Use a four-part donation screen


Every item should pass four checks before entering the closet.


**1. Is it something students currently need?**


Check inventory before adding another item to an oversupplied category.


**2. Is it current enough to wear now?**


K-State asks for clothing purchased within approximately the past five years.


**3. Is it immediately wearable?**


UHCL asks for clean, pressed, ready-to-wear clothing without stains, odors, tears, missing buttons, loose hems, or needed alterations.


**4. Does it fit a professional use case?**


Virginia Tech accepts business-professional and business-casual items but does not accept casual, athletic, or formal social attire.


[Rutgers](https://careers.rutgers.edu/students-alumni/online-tools-and-resources/career-closet/support-career-closet) takes a similar approach and asks donors to provide clothing that is clean, neat, and ready to wear, even specifically reminding donors to inspect dress-shirt collars for staining or yellowing.


Being selective is not being ungrateful to donors. It protects staff time and makes the closet better for students.


## How Should Career Centers Decide Who Can Use the Closet and How Much They Can Take?


Use the least restrictive rule that your inventory and funding can support. For donated clothing, a student ID plus an item or outfit limit is often enough. Use need-based eligibility when money, scholarships, or externally restricted funds require it. Keep an exception route for students whose circumstances do not fit the standard policy.


Universities already use several approaches.


Kansas State makes its Career Closet available to **all K-State students** and typically allows up to three items depending on inventory.


The University of Florida makes its closet available to **all current students and alumni up to one year after graduation** . Students can currently receive one full professional outfit, but the center explicitly invites students who need additional clothing to contact the team for further support.


Virginia Tech allows one full professional outfit per academic year and one shopping appointment, while also offering pop-up and private shopping events.


UGA uses a different rule for its $200 clothing scholarship because money is being distributed. Students must have documented financial need through the Office of Student Financial Aid.


These examples suggest a useful distinction:


**Donated inventory:** broad access + reasonable quantity limits.


**Financial assistance:** eligibility criteria when funding requires them.


Avoid asking students to repeatedly demonstrate financial hardship simply to take a donated shirt or pair of trousers unless there is a clear institutional reason to do so.


That friction matters because students already fail to discover or use available support.


The career closet should not become another resource students find only after they needed it.


## When Should Career Closets Be Open and Promoted?


Career closets should increase visibility and access before predictable demand spikes, not maintain identical hours throughout the semester. Career fairs, recruiting cycles,[mock interviews](https://www.hiration.com/blog/mock-interview-rubric-feedback-career-advisors-higher-ed/) , conferences, presentations, and internship starts give teams clear signals for when students are most likely to need clothing.


The University of Florida already adjusts closet availability around Career Prep Week and Career Week.


Texas A&M has taken the closet directly to students through an engineering-complex pop-up before a career fair where professional attire is required.


The operating model can be straightforward.


Timing Career Closet action


4-6 weeks before major fair Audit high-demand sizes and purchase critical gaps


3-4 weeks before Add closet information to fair registration and prep communications


2 weeks before Run main pop-up or increase appointments


1 week before Add extended hours and targeted reminders


1-2 days before Reserve capacity for urgent needs


Event day Consider a limited emergency rack or pop-up if appropriate


After event Record unmet size/item demand and restock before the next recruiting period


Do the same at an individual level. A student booking an interview appointment can receive a closet link.


A student registering for a career fair can see available clothing options immediately.


A faculty member assigning professional presentations can receive a referral link to share with students.


A student accepted to a[career trek](https://www.hiration.com/blog/career-treks-preparation/) , conference, case competition, or employer visit can receive the information automatically.


This is more effective than promoting the closet as a standalone campus service.


## How Can Career Centers Reach Students Who Cannot Visit the Closet During Office Hours?


Career centers should provide at least one route beyond scheduled daytime appointments. Drop-ins, pop-ups, online requests, home delivery, or campus-partner events can extend access to commuting, working, caregiving, online, and time-constrained students without requiring the main closet to remain open constantly.


UC Clermont offers a particularly useful example.


Students can shop in person, make an appointment, or submit an online request. The university says students who cannot come to campus can have their selected professional clothing **shipped directly to their home** .


Virginia Tech combines individual appointments with pop-up shops and private shopping events for student organizations, cultural centers, academic units, and other campus groups.


Those models solve different access problems.


Career centers do not necessarily need longer hours every day. They need **more than one way into the service.**


## How Can Career Centers Connect the Closet to Career Preparation Rather Than Just Clothing?


Career centers should position the closet as one step in a larger preparation path. A student visiting for interview clothing may also need a resume review, interview practice, employer research, or[career-fair strategy](https://www.hiration.com/blog/college-career-fairs-guide/) . The closet creates a natural moment to route students toward those services without turning the visit into a mandatory advising appointment.


A closet visit can trigger a lightweight preparation check:


**What are you preparing for?**


- Interview
- Career fair
- Internship
- Employer visit
- [Networking event](https://www.hiration.com/blog/career-centers-teaching-student-networking-higher-ed/)
- Presentation
- Graduate-school interview
- Conference
- First day or week at work


Then connect the visit to whatever the student is preparing for.


A student picking up interview clothing may also benefit from mock interview practice.


Career-fair visitors can be directed to employer research and[fair-preparation resources](https://www.hiration.com/blog/preparing-first-generation-students-career-fairs-higher-ed/) , while students starting internships may need guidance on building several business-casual outfits rather than choosing one formal look.


The visit reason can also improve inventory planning. Consistent demand before career fairs may justify larger pre-fair pop-ups and deeper inventory during those weeks.


Frequent requests from students beginning internships could point to a need for more versatile business-casual separates or more flexible item limits.


Keep these referrals useful and optional. The closet should make the next relevant step easier, not turn clothing access into another required career-center appointment.


## How Can a Small Career Team Run a Career Closet Without Adding Too Much Staff Work?


Career centers can separate professional judgment from routine closet operations. Student employees, interns, ambassadors, and trained volunteers can manage intake, tagging, inventory, merchandising, checkout, and basic styling while professional staff own policy, purchasing, difficult cases, partnerships, and program evaluation.


Kansas State provides a practical example.


Its 2026 Career Closet Intern role includes managing donation intake, sorting and classifying garments, maintaining the closet, updating the physical layout, coordinating displays and promotions, helping students select clothing, and supporting clothing drives and pop-ups.


The position is designed for approximately **10-15 hours per week** , with additional hours around events.


The[University of Hartford](https://www.hartford.edu/student-life/career-services/student-resources/career-closet.aspx/) also uses student ambassadors to help track inventory, sort and tag donations, and manage checkout.


A simple staffing split could be:


### Student staff or volunteers


- Receive and inspect donations
- Tag sizes and categories
- Update inventory
- Reset racks
- Steam or prepare garments
- Check items in and out
- Flag low-stock categories
- Assist during pop-ups
- Record unsuccessful size requests


### Career-center staff


- Set access policies
- Review purchasing priorities
- Handle exceptions
- Coordinate employer and alumni partners
- Connect the program to recruiting calendars
- Review semester data
- Decide which inventory or processes should change


This prevents advisors from spending professional staff hours sorting donated trousers while still keeping the service connected to the[center's broader career strategy](https://www.hiration.com/blog/career-center-strategy-framework-higher-ed/) .
